3.add: The familiar association of ITD with horizontal direction and ILD with vertical direction is a useful specialization, and ILD also carries an azimuthal component.

4.add: The response boundary and the smaller best area describe different aspects of selectivity, with the best area marking the positions that evoke maximal responses.

third_paragraph.6: A space-specific neuron therefore represents preferred ITD and preferred ILD separately, and it fires most strongly when both cues are favorable. The experiments separate how each cue is represented from how the two representations jointly determine the output.

7.add: Its monaural output is subsequently compared with information from the other ear, and the stable ITD peak shows that the timing pathway continued to function.

8.add: The final spatial response combines the two pathways, with the NM pathway carrying timing and the NA pathway carrying level.

third_paragraph.9: The anatomical separation is compatible with parallel timing and level computations. The phase-locking, rate-level, binaural and inactivation experiments connect these structures to particular acoustic variables, with NM and NL in the timing pathway and NA in the level pathway.

10.add: A phase histogram measures temporal alignment, so it describes timing in NM, and sensitivity to differences between the two ears arises later when inputs from both sides are compared.

11.add: NM emphasizes timing and NA emphasizes level, and the monaural level-sensitive discharge of NA provides input for later comparison between the ears.

12.add: Phase locking declines in quality with frequency, and rate threshold and timing sensitivity are different response measurements, since phase organization could be detected below the level at which a clear increase in average rate appeared.

13.add: The NM recordings identify this loss as a functional property of transmission at the first central relay.

14.add: Anatomical tracing establishes the order of the projections, and the paired frequency-response measurements establish the functional matching needed by a timing comparator.

15.add: A delay line is a pathway whose travel time changes with position, and the dorsal and ventral entry of the two inputs places the axons from the two ears on opposite sides of the nucleus.

18.add: Internodal spacing of about 60 µm inside the nucleus and conduction velocities near 3 to 5 m/s are observations from anatomy and physiology that fit this proposal.

third_paragraph.22: The recording trajectory crossed frequency laminae and sampled the tonotopic organization of the population. Connectivity to the external nucleus was established separately with tracer measurements.
third_paragraph.23: The representation is a map of a computed binaural timing variable distributed across frequency channels. ILD selectivity and broader integration produce the restricted spatial receptive fields of the external nucleus.

24.add: The labeled cells lay in an array that crossed frequency laminae, as expected for convergence of different frequency channels onto one space-specific neuron.

25.add: Cell-count distributions locate the populations that project to each target, and the distributions shifted with the timing preference of the target.

26.add: Convergence across frequency channels therefore suppresses the repeated peaks that each narrowband channel produces, and the principal peak survives because all components agree on it.

27.add: The joint presentation favored the common principal delay, which supports a convergence mechanism, and the final selectivity can include inhibitory and spike-generation nonlinearities as well as excitatory agreement.

28.add: A low peak ratio indicates improved single-cell selectivity, and the ratios across the population measure how much ambiguity each ICx cell retains.

29.add: Sharply peaked ILD tuning emerges at later collicular stages from these graded inputs.

31.add: Later pharmacological experiments tested the contribution of GABAergic inhibition and the effects of manipulating the two VLVp populations independently.

32.add: Functional manipulations and receptor-sensitive interventions establish the signs and consequences of the connections that the tracer labeling reveals.

33.add: Recovery of the original ILD dependence indicates a reversible, local manipulation of the VLVp population.

34.add: The unchanged ITD tuning during the same manipulation indicates that the effect is specific to level processing.

35.add: Inactivating one VLVp and increasing the activity of the same population produced opposite changes at large ipsilateral ILDs, which fits opposing inhibitory influences from the two populations.

36.add: The normal preferred direction therefore reflects the combination of timing and level information and is not found by selecting the largest ILD-alone response.

37.add: A sum of frequency-specific ILD preferences predicted much of the ILD-alone field, which supports a contribution from spectral integration.

38.add: Hyperpolarizing responses outside the preferred combination reflect inhibition, so the membrane voltage carries both excitatory and inhibitory influences before thresholding.

39.add: In the multiplicative description the effectiveness of one cue scales with the strength of the other, which yields a restricted combined preference for timing and level.

41.add: Correlation manipulations therefore test the robustness of multiplication, because reducing the timing signal until it is nearly flat leaves little for the multiplicative term to act on.

42.add: Local drug application establishes a receptor-sensitive contribution of GABA-A inhibition, and VLVa timing selectivity was comparatively unaffected.

third_paragraph.43: Cross-frequency convergence and inhibitory suppression jointly support unique broadband timing selectivity. Blocking GABA-A receptors restored secondary peaks for noise, so inhibition contributes to suppressing the repeated matches while frequency-matched excitation supplies the principal timing preference.

44.add: Spike reduction measures the functional contribution of each receptor class to auditory-evoked responses.

45.add: Together with coincidence detection, bilateral inhibition and cross-frequency convergence, synaptic integration supports the sustained spatial signals available for owl orienting.

inserts.title: A receptive field is the region that drives a neuron
paragraphs: A receptive field is the set of stimulus conditions that changes the activity of a neuron. For an auditory space-specific neuron, the conditions are sound locations described by azimuth, the horizontal angle, and elevation, the vertical angle. The receptive field therefore describes where in space a sound must lie to drive the cell.

Knudsen and Konishi moved a loudspeaker around the head of a lightly anesthetized owl in an anechoic chamber. Noise bursts 10 dB above threshold were presented at many positions while extracellular spikes were recorded.

The best area is the subset of positions that evoke maximal responses, and the broader response boundary includes positions that evoke weaker responses. Most fields were vertically elongated, so a neuron specified horizontal direction more narrowly than elevation.
notes: A receptive field is a map of where in space a sound makes a neuron fire.
Definition.
A receptive field is the set of stimulus conditions that changes the activity of a neuron.
For these neurons the conditions are directions in azimuth and elevation.
Method.
A loudspeaker was moved around the head of a lightly anesthetized owl.
The anechoic chamber minimized reflected sound, so the speaker position defined the direction of the sound.
Stimuli.
Noise bursts lasted 100 milliseconds and were delivered 10 decibels above the threshold of each unit.
Best area.
The best area contains the positions that produced maximal responses, and the response boundary is wider.
The two describe different aspects of selectivity.
Shape of the fields.
Most fields were vertically elongated, with widths from 7 to 40 degrees in azimuth and a mean near 25 degrees.
Reading the numbers.
A width of 7 degrees describes a very sharply tuned neuron, and 40 degrees describes a broadly tuned one.
The mean width in azimuth was about 25 degrees.
Selectivity and behavior.
Neither the response boundary nor the best area is itself a behavioral threshold for localizing a sound.

inserts.title: Neighboring neurons represent neighboring locations
paragraphs: A topographic map places neurons with similar preferences next to one another in the tissue. In the auditory midbrain of the owl, the preferred location of a neuron changed in an orderly way along the electrode track.

Best-area azimuth shifted from approximately 60° contralateral in the posterolateral region to 15° ipsilateral anteromedially. Best-area elevation ranged from about +20° down to −90°, with higher directions represented dorsally.

The cochlea represents sound frequency along its length and does not represent location, so the map of space is computed in the brain. The preserved best-area location across tones, clicks, noise and levels indicates that the neurons represent where a sound is and not what it sounds like.
notes: The midbrain contains an orderly map of auditory space, and the map has to be computed.
Topography.
In a topographic map, neighboring neurons have neighboring preferences.
Here the preference is a location in space.
Orderly progression.
Azimuth shifted from about 60 degrees contralateral in the posterolateral region to 15 degrees ipsilateral anteromedially.
Elevation ranged from about plus 20 to minus 90 degrees, with higher directions dorsal.
Overlap.
Neighboring neurons generally had overlapping receptive fields.
Why the map is computed.
The cochlea is organized by sound frequency and not by location.
Location must be derived from differences between the two ears.
Stable location.
Tone bursts, clicks and noise usually preserved the best-area location, and so did a change in level from 10 to 30 decibels above threshold.
Midbrain structure.
The auditory region is called MLD, nucleus mesencephalicus lateralis dorsalis, which is the avian homolog of the inferior colliculus.
Electrode tracks were reconstructed histologically.
Recording position and best area.
The position of each recording was compared with the center of the best area of the neuron.
The orderly relation between the two is the evidence for a map.

inserts.title: A double dissociation separates two pathways
paragraphs: A double dissociation occurs when disrupting one pathway impairs one function and spares another, whereas disrupting a second pathway produces the reverse pattern. The pattern shows that the two functions depend on different pathways. The result is a selective effect on one binaural cue for each nucleus.

Lidocaine injected into nucleus angularis altered the ILD tuning of a space-specific midbrain neuron and left the ITD peak stable. Injected into nucleus magnocellularis, it altered ITD tuning and left the preferred ILD approximately unchanged.

Recovery after each injection and histology of the injection sites linked the changes to a reversible, localized manipulation. The two cochlear nuclei therefore feed separate processing streams for timing and level before the cues converge in the midbrain.
notes: Two manipulations with opposite selective effects show that two functions rely on separate pathways.
Logic.
Disrupting pathway one changes function A and spares function B.
Disrupting pathway two changes function B and spares function A.
Angularis.
Lidocaine in nucleus angularis shifted the ILD response of a midbrain neuron.
The ITD response peak remained essentially stable.
Magnocellularis.
Lidocaine in nucleus magnocellularis altered ITD tuning.
The preferred ILD remained approximately unchanged.
Controls.
Recordings before injection, during the effect and after recovery supplied a temporal control.
Injection-site histology checked the location of each manipulation.
Interpretation.
The timing and level cues are processed in separate streams from the cochlear nuclei onward.
Why a double dissociation is strong evidence.
A single inactivation could reflect a nonspecific impairment of the animal.
Opposite selective effects from two sites make the pathways functionally distinct.
Limits of the manipulation.
The result separates the two pathways at the cochlear nuclei.
The final spatial response still requires both pathways, and the nuclei converge later in the midbrain.

inserts.title: Phase locking keeps spike timing within a sound cycle
paragraphs: A sound wave repeats in cycles, and phase is the position within a cycle. A phase-locked neuron fires at a preferred phase, so its spike times carry the timing of the waveform. Phase locking is the property that allows timing information to be carried by spike times.

Sullivan and Konishi grouped spike times from NM neurons into period histograms that align successive stimulus cycles. NM neurons retained phase locking at frequencies up to 9 kHz. A period histogram of a strongly phase-locked neuron has a sharp peak at one phase.

Spikes could occur on different cycles and still cluster at one position within the cycle, so timing survives without one spike per cycle. The narrow rate-level functions of NM suggest that its output is specialized for transmitting timing.
notes: Phase locking is the way a neuron preserves the fine timing of a sound wave in its spikes.
Phase.
A sound wave repeats in cycles, and phase is the position within a cycle.
Phase-locked firing.
A phase-locked neuron fires at a preferred phase of the wave.
Its spike times therefore carry the timing of the waveform.
Period histograms.
Spike times were grouped into histograms that align successive cycles of the tone.
A peak in the histogram shows concentration at one phase.
Frequency range.
NM neurons retained phase locking at frequencies up to 9 kilohertz.
Missing cycles.
A neuron need not fire on every cycle.
Timing information survives when spikes on different cycles occupy the same position within the cycle.
Cycles and spikes.
A tone of high frequency has many cycles per second, and a neuron firing a few spikes per second cannot respond to each one.
Phase locking means the spikes that do occur fall at a consistent phase.
Nucleus magnocellularis.
NM is a cochlear nucleus that receives auditory-nerve input.
Its neurons transmit timing to nucleus laminaris, where the two ears are compared.

inserts.title: Vector strength measures how tightly spikes align
paragraphs: Vector strength is a number between zero and one that describes how tightly spikes cluster at one phase of a repeating sound. Values near one mean that spikes occur at nearly the same phase, and values near zero mean that the phases are dispersed.

Köppl measured vector strength in single auditory-nerve fibers across frequency and level. Phase locking extended to approximately 10 kHz, with its quality declining as frequency rose and showing a plateau around 1.5 to 3 kHz.

Phase organization could be detected below the level at which average spike rate clearly increased, so timing and rate carry different information. The auditory nerve therefore supplies the brainstem with a temporal code for ITD processing.
notes: Vector strength gives one number for the quality of phase locking.
Scale.
A value near one means spikes fall at nearly the same phase of the sound.
A value near zero means the spike phases are spread across the cycle.
Recordings.
Single auditory-nerve fibers were recorded with calibrated tones, and frequency and level were varied.
Frequency dependence.
Phase locking extended to approximately 10 kilohertz.
Its quality declined with frequency, with a plateau around 1.5 to 3 kilohertz.
Rate and timing.
Phase organization could be detected below the sound level at which average spike rate began to increase clearly.
Rate threshold and timing sensitivity are different measurements.
Role.
The temporal code in the auditory nerve provides the brainstem with the information needed for ITD processing.
Why high frequencies matter.
The owl localizes sounds that include frequencies up to several kilohertz.
Phase locking in the nerve must extend into that range to support ITD.
Comparing measures.
Vector strength describes timing, whereas average spike rate describes how many spikes occur.
The two measures were compared as frequency and sound level changed.

inserts.title: A delay line makes travel time depend on position
paragraphs: A delay line is a pathway in which travel time changes with position along its length. Axons that enter a nucleus from opposite borders create such an arrangement when each input reaches successive neurons at systematically different times.

Carr and Konishi labeled NM axons with HRP and followed them through serial sections. Ipsilateral branches approached the dorsal border of laminaris, and contralateral branches approached the ventral border. The published reconstruction includes a scale bar of 1 mm.

A neuron deep in the nucleus receives the ipsilateral input after a longer path than the contralateral input, whereas a neuron near the dorsal edge shows the reverse. Position within laminaris therefore corresponds to a particular difference in arrival time.
notes: A delay line converts position into time, which is the anatomical basis for mapping ITD.
Definition.
A delay line is a pathway in which travel time changes with position.
Inputs arriving from opposite borders create opposing gradients.
Tracing.
HRP injected into NM labels axons that can be followed through serial sections after a histochemical reaction.
Opposite borders.
Each NM neuron sends branches to laminaris on both sides.
Ipsilateral afferents approach the dorsal border, and contralateral afferents approach the ventral border.
Consequence for arrival times.
Deeper neurons receive the ipsilateral input later than the contralateral input.
Neurons near the dorsal edge receive the contralateral input later.
Physiology.
Recordings of spike timing at different depths test whether conduction time actually changes along the projection.
Visualizing a projection.
HRP is a tracer that makes a projection visible after a histochemical reaction.
Serial brain sections allow an axon to be followed through the tissue.
Opposing arrangement.
The published reconstruction preserves the opposing arrangement of the ipsilateral and contralateral inputs.
The anatomy supplies the layout, and the physiology that follows tests whether delays change along the axons.

inserts.title: Phase repeats each cycle, so phase appears to wrap
paragraphs: Phase is measured within one cycle of a tone, so it returns to its starting value after a complete period. A delay that keeps increasing therefore produces a phase that repeats. The same logic applies to every frequency, but the length of the period depends on the frequency of the tone.

At 4 kHz the period is 250 µs, and at 5.5 kHz it is approximately 182 µs. In a 7-kHz region, abrupt phase jumps corresponded to crossing into the next stimulus cycle. The period is the reciprocal of the frequency, and a higher frequency has a shorter period.

Unwrapping the phase shows a continuous gradient of delay with depth. The mean phase changed regularly across the nucleus, which indicates orderly neural delays and not independent timing at each recording site.
notes: Phase wraps because it is defined within one cycle, and delay keeps increasing across cycles.
Period.
A 4-kilohertz tone has a period of 250 microseconds.
A 5.5-kilohertz tone has a period of approximately 182 microseconds.
Wrapping.
After a delay of one full period the phase returns to the same value.
A measurement of phase alone therefore cannot say how many complete periods have elapsed.
Phase jumps.
In a 7-kilohertz region, abrupt apparent jumps in phase corresponded to crossing into the next stimulus cycle.
Continuous gradient.
After allowing for the repeating cycles, mean phase changed regularly with depth.
The gradient indicates orderly neural delays across the nucleus.
Why it matters.
A gradient of delay with depth is the physiological requirement for a delay line.
Experimental design.
A tone was presented to one ear, and the mean phase of intracellularly recorded spikes was measured at different depths.
A regular change in phase with depth indicates a change in conduction time.
Interpreting jumps.
An abrupt jump of a full cycle does not indicate an abrupt change in delay.
It reflects the repetition of phase.

inserts.title: Coincidence detectors fire when inputs arrive together
paragraphs: A coincidence detector responds strongly when two inputs arrive within a short interval and weakly when they arrive apart. Such a neuron signals simultaneity of its inputs. In the owl the two inputs come from the two ears through the delay-line axons of nucleus magnocellularis.

Carr and Konishi stimulated each ear separately and then varied ITD during binaural stimulation. At a favorable delay the response of one neuron rose to 1107 spikes, compared with 393 and 360 for the two separate-ear conditions. The recordings were made inside the nucleus laminaris with intracellular electrodes.

The binaural response was much larger than either monaural response, and unfavorable delays gave much smaller responses. The response therefore depended on the relative timing of the inputs from the two ears.
notes: A coincidence detector reports that two signals arrived at the same moment.
Definition.
Firing is enhanced when two inputs arrive within a short interval.
Inputs that arrive apart give a smaller response.
Procedure.
Each ear was stimulated separately, and then ITD was varied during binaural stimulation.
Recordings were intracellular.
Example neuron.
At a favorable delay of 30 microseconds the neuron fired 1107 spikes.
Separate stimulation of each ear gave 393 and 360 spikes.
Dependence on timing.
The same neuron responded much less at unfavorable delays.
Link to the delay line.
Opposing delay gradients mean that an external ITD compensates the internal delay at one position, where the two inputs coincide.
Intracellular recording.
Recording inside the cell shows the response of an identified neuron to each ear separately and to both ears together.
Across the study.
Favorable binaural responses were roughly twice monaural responses.
The enhancement fits coincidence-sensitive integration of input from the two ears.

inserts.title: Periodic channels confuse delays one period apart
paragraphs: A narrowband channel is driven by a tone, which repeats every period. The same phase relationship between the two ears recurs whenever the interaural delay changes by one period of the tone. The firing rate of the neuron therefore peaks repeatedly as the delay changes.

At 4 kHz the period is 250 µs, so alignment recurs at delays separated by 250 µs. Carr and Konishi measured repeated firing maxima across a range of imposed delays, and the spacing of the maxima matched the stimulus frequency.

Phase ambiguity is the inability of one narrowband channel to identify a unique ITD from its firing rate. Information from other frequency channels, which have different periods, can identify the one delay that all channels share.
notes: A single frequency channel cannot tell apart delays that differ by a whole number of periods.
Periodic input.
A tone repeats every period, so the same alignment between the ears occurs again after each period.
Example.
At 4 kilohertz the period is 250 microseconds.
Alignment recurs at delays separated by 250 microseconds.
Measurement.
Firing was measured across a range of imposed delays.
The repeated maxima had spacing consistent with the stimulus frequency.
Ambiguity.
A single narrowband channel cannot assign one unique ITD from its firing rate.
Resolution.
Channels at other frequencies have different periods, so only the true delay is shared by all of them.
Delay curves.
A delay curve plots firing against imposed interaural delay.
Different neurons differed in preferred timing and in the depth of modulation.
Beyond the physiological range.
Repeated opportunities for alignment occur at delays beyond the strongest peak near the physiological range.
The ambiguity belongs to the narrow frequency channel and not to the whole system.

inserts.title: Isofrequency laminae stack frequency channels
paragraphs: An isofrequency lamina is a sheet of neurons with similar frequency tuning. Moving an electrode across laminae samples neurons with different best frequencies. Frequency tuning is the property that organizes the array.

Wagner and colleagues advanced electrodes dorsoventrally through the central nucleus of the inferior colliculus. In a representative penetration, best frequency rose from approximately 500 Hz to 10 kHz with depth. The recording sites were reconstructed histologically in the experiment.

A neuron in each lamina has its own period, so the array provides a range of frequencies for testing whether different channels share a common delay. The penetration samples the tonotopic order of the population. The tonotopic order is the basis on which the timing relation across frequency can then be compared.
notes: The central nucleus of the inferior colliculus is organized in frequency layers.
Laminae.
An isofrequency lamina is a sheet of neurons with similar frequency tuning.
Different laminae have different best frequencies.
Penetrations.
Electrodes were advanced dorsoventrally through the central nucleus.
Reconstructed positions established the orientation of the arrays.
Tonotopy.
In a representative penetration best frequency rose monotonically from approximately 500 hertz to 10 kilohertz.
Why frequency diversity matters.
Each lamina has a different period, so testing across laminae asks whether channels share one delay.
A shared preferred phase would not be enough.
Sampling.
The trajectory samples the population and does not follow a single neuron through every channel.
Relation to arrays.
The earlier slides described neurons that share a timing relation across frequency.
An array is a group of neurons arranged across laminae with a common timing relation.
Anatomical orientation.
Seven penetrations were reconstructed histologically, which established the orientation of the arrays in the colliculus.

inserts.title: Broadband sounds contain many frequency periods
paragraphs: A tone contains a single period, whereas broadband noise contains many frequency components with different periods. Each component produces its own repeated pattern of delay matches. The comparison tests how a neuron treats a single frequency period relative to the combined periods of a broad sound.

Takahashi and Konishi compared ICx delay curves evoked by a best-frequency tone with curves evoked by broadband noise in the same neuron. Tones produced a principal peak and secondary peaks, and noise greatly reduced the secondary peaks.

Repeated peaks of different components fall at different delays and do not coincide, but the true delay is common to all components. Summing across frequency channels therefore reinforces the shared delay and diminishes the repeated matches. The principal peak is the one that all frequency components share.
notes: Natural sounds are broadband, which helps remove the ambiguity of single channels.
Tone and noise.
A tone has one period, and broadband noise has many components with different periods.
Same neuron.
Recording the same ICx neuron with both stimuli holds the recording site constant.
Result.
Tones produced a principal peak with repeated secondary peaks.
Noise greatly reduced the secondary peaks while keeping the timing near the principal peak.
Reason.
Secondary peaks of different components occur at different delays.
The true delay is the one that every component shares.
Convergence.
Input from many frequency channels onto one neuron reinforces the shared delay.
Same neuron comparison.
Each neuron served as its own control, so differences between tone and noise belong to the stimulus and not to the sample of cells.
The best-frequency tone was matched to the neuron.
Ambiguity resolution.
A tone gives a principal peak and secondary peaks.
Broadband input keeps the principal peak and greatly weakens the secondary peaks.

inserts.title: Half-maximum ILD summarizes a monotonic level curve
paragraphs: A monotonic response keeps rising or keeps falling as a stimulus parameter increases. When the parameter is the interaural level difference, the curve has no peak, so a summary other than a preferred value is needed.

Manley and colleagues described each VLVp response by its half-maximum point, the ILD at which firing reaches half of its maximum. Dorsal sites had more contralaterally biased half-maximum points, and ventral sites shifted toward ipsilateral values.

The half-maximum point is therefore a position along the binaural level axis, and it varies in an orderly way with recording position. Some cells changed their half-maximum point by 2 dB or less when average binaural level rose by 10 dB.
notes: A curve without a peak can still be summarized by a single criterion point.
Monotonic curves.
A monotonic response keeps rising or falling with the stimulus parameter.
VLVp responses to interaural level difference were largely of this type.
Half-maximum point.
The half-maximum point is the ILD at which firing reaches half of its maximum.
It marks where along the level axis the response changes.
Anatomical order.
Dorsal sites had more contralaterally biased half-maximum points.
Ventral sites shifted toward ipsilateral values.
Level stability.
Some cells changed their half-maximum point by 2 decibels or less when average binaural level rose by 10 decibels.
Comparison with spatial maps.
The ordering concerns response thresholds on a level axis and differs from a map of receptive-field centers.
Sequential sites.
Sequential recording sites within a penetration were compared to test for an anatomical order.
The ordered criterion is the result.
Comparison with direction.
The map is an ordering of thresholds along a level axis and is not a map of locations in space.

inserts.title: Subthreshold potentials precede spike generation
paragraphs: A neuron integrates synaptic inputs as changes in membrane voltage before it produces any spikes. Depolarization moves the voltage toward threshold, and hyperpolarization moves it away. Subthreshold recording therefore gives access to the inputs that the neuron receives, which spikes alone do not show.

Peña and Konishi recorded identified ICx neurons intracellularly and presented ITD and ILD pairs. Responses were depolarizing near a preferred combination and hyperpolarizing outside it, with spike output restricted to a smaller center. The spike output is a thresholded version of the membrane response.

Intracellular recording therefore separates the integration of timing and level from the later thresholding that produces spikes. A depolarization at an unfavorable cue pair may stay below threshold and produce no spikes. The neurons were labeled with neurobiotin, which identified them as ICx cells.
notes: Membrane voltage shows the result of synaptic integration before spikes are produced.
Membrane potential.
Depolarization moves the voltage toward spike threshold.
Hyperpolarization moves it away from threshold.
Recording.
Identified ICx neurons were recorded intracellularly and labeled with neurobiotin.
Broadband noise bursts 100 milliseconds long were presented 30 decibels above threshold.
Tuning.
Combinations of ITD and ILD near the preferred pair gave depolarization.
Combinations outside it gave hyperpolarization.
Spikes.
The spike output formed a smaller excitatory center surrounded by reduced firing.
Mixture of inputs.
The recorded voltage can contain both excitatory and inhibitory influences, so it is not the response of one conductance.
Why record intracellularly.
Extracellular spikes show only the output of a neuron.
The membrane potential shows the sum of excitatory and inhibitory inputs before the spike threshold is applied.
Stimulus pairs.
Pairs of ITD and ILD were tested systematically.
Each pair gave a depolarizing or a hyperpolarizing response, and the pattern across pairs forms the tuning.

inserts.title: Multiplication makes one cue scale the other
paragraphs: In an additive interaction the effects of two cues sum, whereas in a multiplicative interaction the effectiveness of one cue depends on the strength of the other. A multiplicative neuron responds strongly only when both cues are favorable. The distinction determines whether a neuron can act as an AND-like detector for the location of a source.

Peña and Konishi arranged subthreshold responses in a matrix of ITD and ILD combinations. A matrix analysis separated the responses into ranked components, and a multiplicative component described most of the response structure.

Multiplication captured the data better than addition. If either cue is absent the product is small, so the response of the neuron is restricted to the combination of timing and level that falls at its preferred location.
notes: Whether timing and level add or multiply determines how a neuron's spatial tuning is shaped.
Addition and multiplication.
With addition the two cue effects sum.
With multiplication the effectiveness of one cue depends on the strength of the other.
The matrix.
Subthreshold responses were arranged by ITD and ILD, so each cell of the matrix is one cue pair.
Analysis.
A matrix analysis separated the responses into ranked components.
A multiplicative component described most of the structure after a constant offset was accounted for.
Result.
Multiplication captured the data better than a simple additive alternative.
Consequence.
If either cue is absent the product is small.
The neuron therefore responds strongly only at the location that favors both timing and level.
Constant offset.
A constant membrane-voltage offset was accounted for before testing the interaction.
The remaining structure was compared with additive and multiplicative accounts.
Level of description.
The result describes a computation at the level of membrane responses.
It does not assign multiplication to one receptor or one dendritic compartment.
